title: Pre-training a 1.11B LLM on a 6 GB Laptop GPU — Measured, Not Claimed
gist: A hobbyist, working with Claude, combined published memory-saving techniques (BAdam block-coordinate descent, CPU offload, BitNet ternary weights, tied embeddings, gradient checkpointing, chunked cross-entropy). The stack fits a 1.11B-parameter gated-DeltaNet hybrid for pretraining in 4.51 GB on a 6 GB RTX 4050 laptop GPU, about 6.5x the largest model a standard script can fit. The author stresses that fitting a model is not the same as training it: compute is already at the GEMM ceiling, and a proper Chinchilla-style run would take about 375 days. Nothing above 48M parameters was trained to convergence, and the article gives inconsistent throughput and token figures (1,579 vs ~1,100 tok/s; 33B vs 36B tokens).

insights.claim: Combining six published techniques (BAdam block-coordinate descent, CPU weight offload, BitNet b1.58 ternary weights, tied embeddings, gradient checkpointing, chunked cross-entropy) let a 1.11B-parameter LLM be pretrained within 4.51 GB peak VRAM on a 6 GB RTX 4050 laptop GPU at 4,096 context.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Billion-parameter pretraining is now memory-feasible on sub-$1,000 consumer laptops, which weakens the narrative that only datacenter GPUs can host LLM training.
insights.locator: The Headline Numbers (Measured on RTX 4050 6 GB)

insights.claim: On the same 6 GB card at 4,096 context, a standard training script tops out at about 243M parameters before spilling into system RAM, while the combined memory stack reaches about 1.58B. That is roughly a 6.5x increase in the largest model that fits.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Software-level memory tricks are multiplying the effective capacity of installed consumer GPU hardware, and that extends the useful life of low-VRAM SKUs for AI work.
insights.quote: ~243M on a standard script, ~1.58B with the stack — about 6.5×.
insights.locator: What You Get Without Any of This

insights.claim: The 6.5x memory gain comes from the pretraining stack, not the model architecture: a plain 1.07B transformer runs under the same stack in 4.04 GB, almost the same as the recurrent hybrid.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: The gain is architecture-agnostic, so it could be applied broadly to ordinary transformer training rather than only to niche recurrent models.
insights.quote: The 6.5× comes from the pretraining stack, not from the architecture
insights.locator: What the table does not show

insights.claim: Block-coordinate descent (BAdam) trains one block at a time and keeps optimizer state only for the active block, which cuts optimizer-state memory by about 8x.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Optimizer state is a dominant memory cost in training, and compressing it is a key lever for low-memory training hardware.
insights.locator: The 5-Technique Stack That Made Pretraining Possible

insights.claim: BitNet b1.58 ternary weights compress weight tensors only 2.33x in practice (int8 storage plus a per-matrix fp32 scale), against a theoretical 20x. They give no VRAM saving during training because fp32 shadow weights stay resident; the benefit is limited to checkpoint size and inference memory.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: The headline 1.58-bit compression mostly helps inference and edge deployment, not training economics, so ternary claims about training should be discounted.
insights.quote: No training VRAM win: fp32 shadow weights stay resident for gradient updates. Ternary saves checkpoint size and inference memory only.

insights.claim: Ternary (BitNet b1.58) models must be trained from scratch with quantization-aware training and a straight-through estimator. Post-hoc quantization loses the learned dynamics, and fresh layers can collapse to zero at initialization unless the trunk is warm-started from a pretrained checkpoint.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Existing models cannot be cheaply converted to ternary, so 1.58-bit efficiency gains need new training runs, which slows their adoption.

insights.claim: In ternary quantization, finer group-wise scales lost to a single per-tensor scale on quality. About 35% of ternary weights round to exactly zero, spread across rows rather than collapsing whole rows.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Natural sparsity of about one-third in ternary weights is a possible hook for sparse-inference hardware and kernels.

insights.claim: The largest single memory consumer in small-model LLM training is not the weights but the cross-entropy loss over the vocabulary. At 4,096 positions x 50,257 vocabulary it takes about 1,500 MB, roughly 3x the ternary weights (~960 MB at 48M), and chunked loss computation over 512 positions at a time saves about 1.5 GB.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Vocabulary size and context length drive training memory more than parameter count at small scale, so efficiency tooling that targets the loss layer has outsized value.
insights.quote: The largest consumer is not the model — it's the cross-entropy over the vocabulary (~3× the weights).

insights.claim: Tied embeddings and CPU offload were previously incompatible because the offload system assigns each parameter to exactly one block. The fix pins the shared vocabulary table in VRAM (about 206-250 MB at 1B scale), and combined with chunked cross-entropy, a 1.11B tied, offloaded run fit in 4.85 GB (79% of 6 GB) where it had previously run out of memory.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Much of the efficiency gain comes from engineering integration of known techniques rather than new algorithms, so it is replicable and hard to protect as a moat.
insights.locator: Two of these did not previously work together

insights.claim: The stack contains no new algorithms. Every component is published work, and the contribution is making them run together and measuring what that costs.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Cheap-training advances are coming from open-source composition work by individuals using AI assistants, which diffuses capability quickly and commoditizes it.
insights.quote: No new algorithms — every piece is published and attributed. The work was making them run together and measuring what that costs.
insights.locator: The 5-Technique Stack That Made Pretraining Possible

insights.claim: A non-specialist said he built the 1B-on-a-laptop training stack by subscribing to Claude and iterating through prompting and testing, after finding only consensus advice that an A100 was required.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: AI coding assistants are letting non-experts produce ML systems engineering, which widens the builder base and supports demand for assistant subscriptions.
insights.quote: So being 'broke', I did the only thing I could do — subscribe to Claude and try to find a way
insights.locator: I looked everywhere to be able

themes.theme: Compute wall: fitting is not training

insights.claim: Although a 1.11B model fits in 6 GB, pretraining it properly on an RTX 4050 laptop would take about 375 days for roughly 33-36B tokens. Memory tricks raise what can be held, but they do not touch the arithmetic throughput wall.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Consumer hardware makes LLM training memory-feasible but not time-feasible, so demand for datacenter compute FLOPs is not threatened by these tricks.
insights.quote: The ceiling this stack raises is what you can hold; the wall it does not touch is arithmetic.

insights.claim: Matrix multiplications run at 100.6% of the RTX 4050's measured GEMM peak but make up only 33% of a training step. The rest is small memory-bound operations (36%), sequential scan stepping (15%) and data movement caused by offloading (15%).
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Memory bandwidth and data movement, not raw FLOPs, dominate step time on constrained hardware, which favours higher-bandwidth memory products.

insights.claim: All remaining optimizations, added up optimistically, would improve pretraining speed by only 20-25%, cutting a 375-day 1.11B run to about 300 days. The bottleneck is the 36B-token volume, not bad code.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: There is little software headroom left on consumer cards, so meaningful training speedups require more hardware compute.
insights.quote: The year is not bad code — it is 36 billion tokens.

insights.claim: Projected by linear extrapolation, not measurement, the memory stack would let a 24 GB RTX 3090/4090 pretrain about a 7.5B model and finish a 5B Chinchilla-style pretrain in about 18 days. The projections are about 40 days at 3.5B on 16 GB, 75 days at 2.5B on 12 GB and 160 days at 1.5B on 8 GB.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: If these projections hold, high-VRAM consumer cards such as the 24 GB 4090 class become practical for small-model pretraining, which supports prosumer GPU demand. The author labels every row except 6 GB as unmeasured.
insights.quote: At 24 GB, a 7B pretrain is ~18 days — actually finishable
insights.locator: What This Means for Your GPU

insights.claim: The author argues the trainable-model ceiling scales linearly with VRAM because the dominant costs (weights and optimizer state) scale with model size and the stack compresses them by fixed ratios, so a 24 GB card fits about 5x the parameters of a 6 GB card.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: VRAM capacity is the key product-segmentation variable for local AI training, which strengthens pricing power on high-VRAM consumer SKUs.
insights.quote: A 24 GB card doesn't just fit "a bit more" — it fits ~5× the parameters of a 6 GB card.
insights.locator: The ceiling is linear in VRAM

insights.claim: On cards with more VRAM, dropping CPU offload removes the PCIe bottleneck for about a 20% speedup, but training then hits the compute wall sooner because matmuls are already at their ceiling.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Beyond memory, raw compute becomes the binding constraint, which keeps the FLOPs-per-dollar race central to GPU value.

insights.claim: The author's rule of thumb for offloaded consumer-GPU training is system RAM of at least 2x GPU VRAM (at least 1.5x without offload); a 1.11B offloaded run parks about 3-4 GB of weights in host RAM.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Local AI training raises DRAM content per PC (32-96 GB recommended), a tailwind for consumer DRAM demand.
insights.quote: Rule of thumb: System RAM ≥ 2× GPU VRAM for offload runs; ≥ 1.5× for no-offload runs.

insights.claim: On Windows, the WDDM display driver model does not raise an out-of-memory error when VRAM is exceeded. It silently spills to system RAM over PCIe at 4-15x slower speeds; a 2.45B model measured 82 s per micro-batch when it spilled.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Windows adds a hidden performance trap for local AI workloads, which favours Linux-based setups for serious consumer-GPU training.

insights.claim: The author's view is that a 6 GB GPU is practical for pretraining models that emit correctly formatted tool calls (about 100-270M parameters, days of training) or hold a coherent conversation (about 270M, around 24 days), but writing trustworthy code is out of reach.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Cheap local pretraining suits narrow agent and tool-use micro-models rather than frontier-capability tasks, and it points to a niche for specialised small models.
insights.locator: What a 6 GB Card Is Good For

themes.theme: Hybrid recurrent architecture and exact recall

insights.claim: The trained model is a reimplemented gated DeltaNet hybrid of 10 recurrent DeltaNet blocks plus 2 sliding-window attention layers (window 128) at layers 3 and 10. Like Mamba, RWKV and RetNet, it has constant-memory inference with no KV cache.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Recurrent-attention hybrids with fixed-memory inference are becoming standard in open work, and they lower inference memory costs for edge deployment.

insights.claim: On a 200-trial synthetic recall probe, a pure DeltaNet trunk recalled exact tokens within 128 tokens only 4-5% of the time. Adding two 128-token sliding-window attention layers raised near-window recall to 35.5% (9x) and far-window recall from 0.5% to 8.5%.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Pure recurrent models are weak at exact retrieval, so hybrids with some attention are likely to win for agentic, coding and grounded-QA use cases.
insights.locator: Why Hybrid Attention? Inference-Time Exact Recall

insights.claim: Pure recurrent models (DeltaNet, Mamba, RWKV) compress history into a fixed state and mathematically cannot recall exact tokens. For coding agents and tool use, this is the difference between hallucinating a function signature and copying it exactly from context.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Architectures without attention face a structural handicap in the agent and coding markets, which limits pure state-space-model disruption of transformers.
insights.quote: this is the difference between "it hallucinates the function signature" and "it copies the exact signature from context."
insights.locator: This means at inference: the hybrid

insights.claim: Adding two windowed attention layers to a recurrent model costs only about 13% more VRAM and about 7% more pretraining step time, and removing attention actually made training 6.4% slower.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Hybrid designs keep exact recall for a small overhead, which makes them an efficient default for small, cheap models.
insights.quote: attention is the cheap part during training
insights.locator: 4 Optimisations Measured Slower Than Doing Nothing

insights.claim: The author's original 'novel' HVN architecture lost by 13% at equal data to the published gated DeltaNet, and the novelty claim was retracted.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Established published architectures are hard to beat for amateurs, so claims of new architectures from small projects deserve skepticism.

insights.claim: For this gated-DeltaNet hybrid, the author recommends about 30 training tokens per parameter rather than Chinchilla's 20. Moving from 20 to 30 tokens/param improved held-out loss by 1.9-3.3% for 50% more tokens, while 30 to 40 gained only about 1.1% for 33% more.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Recurrent hybrids may need about 50% more data than transformers for compute-optimal training, which raises the token and compute bill for these efficient architectures.

insights.claim: Fitting the standard scaling-law form to three model sizes gave a degenerate answer (implying a 1B model needs fewer tokens than parameters), so how the data requirement for recurrent hybrids changes with model size remains unresolved.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Scaling laws for non-transformer architectures are immature, which raises uncertainty around compute planning for alternative architectures.
insights.locator: How this moves with model size

insights.claim: The training script's default data mix caps pretraining at 0.13B tokens because OpenAssistant (only 15.7M tokens) takes a 35% share. A 1B run on defaults would get 270x less data than needed while its loss curve looks healthy from re-reading the same tokens.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: High-quality open pretraining corpora such as FineWeb-Edu are the binding input for cheap training, so data quality and volume remain a scarce asset.
insights.quote: the loss curve looks perfectly healthy while it re-reads the same tokens

insights.claim: torch.compile made training 2.4x slower on this recurrent architecture (20.72 vs 8.66 s/step across 4 independent measurements). Mixture-of-Experts, tensor-train factorisation, weight-shared looped models and chunk-parallel scans also underperformed simple dense baselines.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Mainstream compiler and sparsity optimizations do not transfer cleanly to non-transformer architectures at small scale, which is a tooling gap for alternative model families.

insights.claim: At small scale, Mixture-of-Experts lost to simply scaling the dense model, and a tensor-train factorisation with half the parameters was 22% worse.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Parameter-efficiency tricks that suit frontier-scale models may not pay off for small on-device models.

insights.claim: The Muon optimizer reached the same loss in 1.6x fewer steps but ran about 12% slower per step, and bf16 mixed precision gave a 2-3x speedup with 2x less VRAM on RTX 30/40-series cards.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Newer optimizers like Muon deliver real net training-efficiency gains, adding to the steady software-driven decline in training cost.

insights.claim: A claimed 6.8x CUDA-graph speedup was retracted because it compared one replay with one eager step from the same state. Eight silent bugs were caught by falsifiable tests, including a cache serving untrained weights while aggregate loss still trended down.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: Headline speedup claims in AI efficiency research are often measurement artifacts, so diligence should demand reproducible, falsifiable benchmarks.

insights.claim: Re-running the same model with three different random seeds moved results by 0.089, which is larger than some differences the project reported. Nothing above 48M parameters was trained to convergence, so the scaling statements should not be extrapolated beyond that size.
insights.speaker: Rambarun Komaljeet
insights.so_what: The 1B-on-a-laptop result shows memory feasibility, not a trained 1B model, so it should not be read as proof that competitive models can be trained on consumer hardware.
insights.quote: Nothing above 48M has been trained to convergence here.
